Models, prices and tokens

Source: vignettes/models.Rmd
models.Rmd

Before harnessr sends a request, it looks the model up in its registry. The entry gives the model’s context window and output cap, which size every prompt, and the prices you set, which turn the tokens a request used into dollars and let max_cost_usd hold. The tokens come from a token counter, the same one that measures a prompt before it goes out.

The sections below show what the registry knows about a model and how sure it is, how to add a model and set the prices you pay, what a cost estimate says and when it is NA, and how harnessr counts tokens. Every example runs offline with no API key. The prices in it are illustrative: use your provider’s current prices, in US dollars per million tokens.

Setting up 

library(harnessr)
old <- hr_options(verbose = FALSE)

hr_options() returns the values it replaced, and the last chunk of this guide puts them back with hr_options(old). Every registration below lasts for the R session and changes nothing on disk.

What harnessr knows about a model

hr_models() lists the registry, one row per model, chat models first:

m <- hr_models()
nrow(m)
#> [1] 20
table(m$kind)
#> 
#>      chat embedding 
#>        17         3
m[m$id %in% c("gpt-5.6-terra", "gpt-4o", "gpt-4", "text-embedding-3-small"), ]
#>                        id      kind context_window max_output reasoning
#> 2                   gpt-4      chat           8192       8192     FALSE
#> 7                  gpt-4o      chat         128000      16384     FALSE
#> 17          gpt-5.6-terra      chat        1050000     128000      TRUE
#> 19 text-embedding-3-small embedding           8191          0     FALSE
#>    input_usd_per_1m output_usd_per_1m   as_of cached_input_usd_per_1m
#> 2                NA                NA 2026-08                      NA
#> 7                NA                NA 2026-08                      NA
#> 17               NA                NA 2026-08                      NA
#> 19               NA                NA 2026-08                      NA

harnessr ships 20 models, 17 chat models and 3 embedding models, all OpenAI’s, read from inst/extdata/models.csv when the package loads. For each it ships the limits: context_window (prompt and reply together, in tokens), max_output (the most tokens one reply may have), whether it is a reasoning model and, for an embedding model, its dimensions. The price columns are NA because harnessr ships no prices. The table leaves out supports_temperature and dimensions; hr_model_info() has every field. For a model with no price, as_of is the month its limits were last checked; once you set prices, it is the month of the prices.

gpt-4 lists an output cap equal to its window. A prompt to it still has room: hr_budget() reserves a quarter of the usable window for the reply, not the whole cap:

unlist(hr_budget("gpt-4")[c("context_window", "input", "output")])
#> context_window          input         output 
#>           8192           5529           1843

A tenth of the window is left unused, for error in the token count (see Counting tokens).

One model: hr_model_info()

hr_model_info() returns one model’s entry as a list:

str(hr_model_info("gpt-5.6-terra"))
#> List of 13
#>  $ context_window      : int 1050000
#>  $ max_output          : int 128000
#>  $ input_usd           : num NA
#>  $ output_usd          : num NA
#>  $ reasoning           : logi TRUE
#>  $ supports_temperature: logi FALSE
#>  $ kind                : chr "chat"
#>  $ dimensions          : int NA
#>  $ certain             : logi TRUE
#>  $ as_of               : chr "2026-08"
#>  $ cached_input_usd    : num NA
#>  $ id                  : chr "gpt-5.6-terra"
#>  $ source              : chr "builtin"

Three fields here change how an hr_client() request is built. A model with reasoning = TRUE gets no temperature, and its output cap is raised to at least the reasoning_floor option (2,048 tokens) where the window has room, because its reasoning is billed as output inside the same cap. A model with supports_temperature = FALSE gets no temperature either. A mock or backend handler is given the temperature and cap the call asked for, and passing them on is its business. kind says whether the model answers prompts or returns embeddings.

source says where the entry came from, and certain says whether harnessr knows the model or guessed. harnessr tries five places in order and stops at the first that has the id:

source where the entry came from certain
"registered" hr_register_model() or hr_load_models() in this session TRUE
"builtin" the shipped file TRUE
"alias" a dated or alternative name for a model above, such as "chatgpt-4o-latest" for gpt-4o TRUE
"pattern:..." a family pattern that matches the id, such as ^gpt-4o FALSE
"default" nothing matched: a 128,000-token window and a 4,096-token output cap FALSE

A registered entry wins over a built-in one. An alias takes its target’s entry, a registered one first, and keeps its own name as id:

str(hr_model_info("chatgpt-4o-latest")[c("id", "context_window", "max_output",
                                         "source", "certain")])
#> List of 5
#>  $ id            : chr "chatgpt-4o-latest"
#>  $ context_window: int 128000
#>  $ max_output    : int 16384
#>  $ source        : chr "alias"
#>  $ certain       : logi TRUE

An id the registry does not hold gets a guess, with a warning of class gr_unknown_model. A dated gpt-4o name the registry has not heard of matches the ^gpt-4o pattern:

str(hr_model_info("gpt-4o-2027-01-15")[c("context_window", "max_output",
                                         "source", "certain")])
#> Warning in hr_model_info("gpt-4o-2027-01-15"): Model 'gpt-4o-2027-01-15' is not
#> in the registry; matched family pattern '^gpt-4o' -> 128000-token context,
#> 16384-token output. Verify with hr_model_info('gpt-4o-2027-01-15'), and correct
#> it with hr_register_model() if that is wrong.
#> List of 4
#>  $ context_window: int 128000
#>  $ max_output    : int 16384
#>  $ source        : chr "pattern:^gpt-4o"
#>  $ certain       : logi FALSE

An id that matches no pattern gets the default profile:

str(hr_model_info("acme-chat-7")[c("context_window", "max_output", "source",
                                   "certain")])
#> Warning in hr_model_info("acme-chat-7"): Model 'acme-chat-7' is not in the
#> registry. Falling back to a conservative 128000-token context with a 4096-token
#> output reserve. Register the real limits with hr_register_model('acme-chat-7',
#> context_window = ..., max_output = ...) so budgets and cost estimates are
#> correct.
#> List of 4
#>  $ context_window: int 128000
#>  $ max_output    : int 4096
#>  $ source        : chr "default"
#>  $ certain       : logi FALSE

The warning repeats on every call that names the model, so a run that uses an unknown id says so for each request. Read it as “check this before you trust a budget or a cost”: a guessed window can be far from the real one, and a guessed entry has no price. A typo shows up the same way, and its guess can look right. "gpt-5.6-tera" matches the ^gpt-5\.6 family and gets gpt-5.6-terra’s window, but no price you set for gpt-5.6-terra reaches it.

To stop instead of guessing, set unknown_model_action to "error". A lookup of an unknown id then raises an error of class gr_unknown_model, and so does hr_call() before it sends anything:

prev <- hr_options(unknown_model_action = "error")
tryCatch(hr_model_info("gpt-5.6-tera"),
         gr_unknown_model = function(e) class(e))
#> [1] "gr_unknown_model" "gr_error"         "error"            "condition"
hr_options(prev)

Two limits: hr_model_limits()

hr_model_limits() returns the window and the output cap alone:

hr_model_limits("gpt-4o")
#> $context_window
#> [1] 128000
#> 
#> $output_tokens
#> [1] 16384

The second element is named output_tokens, not max_output as in hr_model_info(). It goes through the same lookup, so an unknown id warns here too.

Adding a model or changing one

hr_register_model() adds an entry or changes one. It does not check the figures with the provider: what you give is what harnessr uses.

A model harnessr does not know

A model behind a company gateway, or a local one, needs both limits. reasoning, supports_temperature, kind and dimensions default to a chat model that takes a temperature:

hr_register_model("gateway-chat", context_window = 200000, max_output = 8192)
str(hr_model_info("gateway-chat")[c("context_window", "max_output", "reasoning",
                                    "supports_temperature", "source", "certain")])
#> List of 6
#>  $ context_window      : int 200000
#>  $ max_output          : int 8192
#>  $ reasoning           : logi FALSE
#>  $ supports_temperature: logi TRUE
#>  $ source              : chr "registered"
#>  $ certain             : logi TRUE

A reasoning model behind the gateway says so, and an embedding model gives its kind and dimensions:

hr_register_model("gateway-reasoner", context_window = 128000, max_output = 16000,
                  reasoning = TRUE, supports_temperature = FALSE)
hr_register_model("gateway-embed", context_window = 8192, max_output = 0,
                  kind = "embedding", dimensions = 1024)

harnessr refuses a chat model whose output cap is as large as its window, because then no room would be left for a prompt:

tryCatch(hr_register_model("too-small", context_window = 4096, max_output = 4096),
         error = conditionMessage)
#> [1] "`max_output` (4096) must be smaller than `context_window` (4096): a model cannot emit its entire context. Set a smaller `max_output` to leave room for a prompt."

A change to one field of a known model

Leave out either limit, and hr_register_model() changes the current entry, built in or registered, keeping every value you leave out. To hold gpt-4o’s replies to 8,000 tokens:

hr_register_model("gpt-4o", max_output = 8000)
str(hr_model_info("gpt-4o")[c("context_window", "max_output", "source")])
#> List of 3
#>  $ context_window: int 128000
#>  $ max_output    : int 8000
#>  $ source        : chr "registered"

The entry is now registered, and it wins over the built-in one until the session ends. A model with no entry to change is an error that says what to give:

tryCatch(hr_register_model("never-seen", max_output = 8000), error = conditionMessage)
#> [1] "Model 'never-seen' is not in the registry, so it has no limits to keep: give both `context_window` and `max_output` to register it."

An alias has no entry of its own, so a change to it is refused with its target named:

tryCatch(hr_register_model("chatgpt-4o-latest", input_usd = 2.5, output_usd = 10),
         error = conditionMessage)
#> [1] "'chatgpt-4o-latest' is an alias of 'gpt-4o'; set the prices on 'gpt-4o'. The alias uses the target's entry."

Prices

Why harnessr ships none

Providers change prices more often than harnessr is released. A price list in the package would be wrong for most of its life, and a wrong price moves the point where max_cost_usd stops a run. A missing price shows: the cost comes out NA. A wrong one gives a figure that looks right. So harnessr ships limits, which change rarely, and you set the prices you pay.

Setting one model’s prices

input_usd and output_usd are US dollars per million tokens. For a known model, the prices are all you give:

# Illustrative figures: use your provider's current prices.
hr_register_model("gpt-4o-mini", input_usd = 0.15, output_usd = 0.60)
str(hr_model_info("gpt-4o-mini")[c("context_window", "max_output", "input_usd",
                                   "output_usd", "as_of", "source")])
#> List of 6
#>  $ context_window: int 128000
#>  $ max_output    : int 16384
#>  $ input_usd     : num 0.15
#>  $ output_usd    : num 0.6
#>  $ as_of         : chr "2026-11"
#>  $ source        : chr "registered"

The model keeps its limits, and the entry is stamped with the current month. Four rules hold for every price:

  • A chat model needs both prices, or neither. Half a price is an error, because a cost with half its price missing cannot be estimated. An embedding model needs only input_usd, since it returns no output tokens.
  • cached_input_usd sets a rate for input the provider served from its prompt cache. Without it, cached input is priced as other input, which never undercounts.
  • A local model costs nothing: give it input_usd = 0 and output_usd = 0. Its cost is then 0, not NA, and the spending limit counts it at zero with no warning.
  • When you change a priced entry, a price you leave out keeps its value. If the change sets only some of the prices, the entry keeps the older month, because the prices you left out are as old as before.
tryCatch(hr_register_model("gpt-4.1-mini", input_usd = 0.40), error = conditionMessage)
#> [1] "Model 'gpt-4.1-mini' has `input_usd` but no `output_usd`. Give both prices (USD per 1M tokens), or neither to register it unpriced, in which case harnessr reports the cost as unknown rather than guessing."
hr_register_model("local-llama", context_window = 32768, max_output = 4096,
                  input_usd = 0, output_usd = 0)
# Illustrative figure.
hr_register_model("gateway-embed", input_usd = 0.05)

Setting many prices from a file: hr_load_models()

hr_load_models() reads a CSV file with a header row and registers each row as hr_register_model() would. id is the only column every file needs, and a blank cell, or NA, means the value is not given:

column what it holds
id the model id, exactly as the API expects it; each id once
input_usd, output_usd price per million tokens, in USD; both for a chat model, or neither
cached_input_usd price per million input tokens served from the provider’s prompt cache
as_of the month you checked the prices, as YYYY-MM; blank stamps the current month, and a later month is an error
context_window, max_output limits in tokens; both for a model harnessr does not know
reasoning, supports_temperature TRUE or FALSE
kind chat or embedding
dimensions how many dimensions an embedding model’s vectors have

?hr_load_models documents the format in full. A row that leaves a limit blank changes the model’s current entry, as hr_register_model() does without one. A row that gives both limits registers the model in full. This file prices two built-in chat models, with a cached input rate for one, and adds a gateway model with its limits:

prices <- file.path(tempdir(), "models-guide-prices.csv")
# Illustrative figures: use your provider's current prices.
writeLines(c(
  "id,input_usd,output_usd,cached_input_usd,context_window,max_output,as_of",
  "gpt-4o,2.50,10.00,1.25,,,",
  "gpt-5.6-terra,2,12,,,,",
  "partner-model,3,15,,200000,8192,2026-10"
), prices)
loaded <- hr_load_models(prices)
loaded
#> [1] "gpt-4o"        "gpt-5.6-terra" "partner-model"
m <- hr_models()
m[m$id %in% loaded, c("id", "context_window", "max_output", "input_usd_per_1m",
                      "output_usd_per_1m", "cached_input_usd_per_1m", "as_of")]
#>               id context_window max_output input_usd_per_1m output_usd_per_1m
#> 9         gpt-4o         128000       8000              2.5                10
#> 19 gpt-5.6-terra        1050000     128000              2.0                12
#> 21 partner-model         200000       8192              3.0                15
#>    cached_input_usd_per_1m   as_of
#> 9                     1.25 2026-11
#> 19                      NA 2026-11
#> 21                      NA 2026-10

hr_load_models() returns, invisibly, the ids it registered, in file order. gpt-4o kept the 8,000-token output cap set earlier, because its row left the limits blank. subset(hr_models(), !is.na(input_usd_per_1m)) lists every model with a price. Check the ids against the ones your runs name: a price set under a misspelt id prices nothing.

harnessr checks the whole file before it registers anything. A file it cannot use stops with an error of class hr_bad_models_file that names the row and column at fault, with row 1 the first row after the header. The registry is left as it was:

bad <- file.path(tempdir(), "models-guide-bad.csv")
writeLines(c("id,input_usd,output_usd", "gpt-4.1,2,8", "gpt-4.1-mini,two,1.6"), bad)
err <- tryCatch(hr_load_models(bad), hr_bad_models_file = function(e) e)
conditionMessage(err)
#> [1] "Models file '/tmp/RtmpcYNwE1/models-guide-bad.csv', row 2, column 'input_usd': 'two' is not a price; give USD per 1M tokens as a number of 0 or more, such as 2.5."
c(row = err$row, column = err$column)
#>         row      column 
#>         "2" "input_usd"
is.na(hr_model_info("gpt-4.1")$input_usd)
#> [1] TRUE

gpt-4.1, on the good first row, has no price: nothing in the file was registered. Loading a file again changes the entries of the models it names as hr_register_model() does, and leaves the others as they are: a value a row leaves blank keeps its current value. Removing a cached rate from the file therefore does not remove it from the registry; register the model in full, with both limits, or start a new session.

Keeping your prices current

A registration lasts for the R session. One file of prices per project sets the same prices in every session, keeps every script on the same figures and puts a date on each:

  1. Keep prices.csv beside your scripts, under version control, with an as_of column holding the month you checked each row.
  2. Load it at the top of each script, or in the project’s .Rprofile, before anything reports a cost.
  3. When your provider changes a price, or the stale warning (below) appears, look up the current prices, change the row and its as_of, and load the file again.
harnessr::hr_load_models("prices.csv")

The file’s commit history records when each price changed, and the as_of column of a cost report says which month’s prices the cost used.

What a cost estimate says: hr_estimate_cost()

hr_estimate_cost() turns token counts into dollars at the model’s prices:

hr_estimate_cost("gpt-4o", input_tokens = 120000, output_tokens = 4000)
#> [1] 0.34

That is 120,000 input tokens at $2.50 per million plus 4,000 output tokens at $10. Vectors of counts are summed, so one call prices a whole run of requests:

hr_estimate_cost("gpt-4o", input_tokens = c(60000, 60000), output_tokens = c(2000, 2000))
#> [1] 0.34

cached_input_tokens says how many of the input tokens the provider served from its prompt cache. gpt-4o has a cached rate here, so 100,000 of the 120,000 are charged at $1.25:

hr_estimate_cost("gpt-4o", 120000, 4000, cached_input_tokens = 100000)
#> [1] 0.215

A model with no cached rate charges them as other input. The estimate is NA, never 0, when the model has no price, when a token count is NA, or when a chat model has no output price and the call has output tokens. A local model at zero prices costs 0:

hr_estimate_cost("gpt-4.1", 120000, 4000)
#> [1] NA
hr_estimate_cost("gpt-4o", NA, 4000)
#> [1] NA
hr_estimate_cost("local-llama", 120000, 4000)
#> [1] 0
hr_estimate_cost("gateway-embed", 1e6)
#> [1] 0.05

detail = TRUE returns a data frame that also says where the figure’s prices came from: priced (whether the model has a price), as_of (the month of the price) and certain (FALSE when the entry was guessed from a pattern or the default):

hr_estimate_cost("gpt-4o", 120000, 4000, detail = TRUE)
#>    model  usd priced   as_of certain
#> 1 gpt-4o 0.34   TRUE 2026-11    TRUE
hr_estimate_cost("acme-chat-7", 120000, 4000, detail = TRUE)
#> Warning in hr_model_info(model): Model 'acme-chat-7' is not in the registry.
#> Falling back to a conservative 128000-token context with a 4096-token output
#> reserve. Register the real limits with hr_register_model('acme-chat-7',
#> context_window = ..., max_output = ...) so budgets and cost estimates are
#> correct.
#>         model usd priced as_of certain
#> 1 acme-chat-7  NA  FALSE  <NA>   FALSE

The second call warned that acme-chat-7 is not in the registry, and its row says why the figure is missing: no price, and an entry that is a guess. Every report of a cost in dollars, such as hr_trace_cost(), carries the same priced, as_of and certain columns, as “What a run records” in vignette("runs") shows for a document run. The figure is an estimate: it uses the token counts you give and the prices you set, and it does not know about a provider’s discounts, minimum charges or taxes.

A model with no price

A request to a chat model with no price is sent. The first request to each such model in a session warns with class hr_unpriced_model, because max_cost_usd cannot hold a cost it cannot compute. The mock client is exempt, so this example uses hr_backend_client(), which wraps an R function as a client that counts as paying:

hr_register_model("unpriced-model", context_window = 128000, max_output = 4096)
backend <- hr_backend_client(function(messages, params) "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars.")

tr <- hr_trace()
res <- hr_call(backend, "What was revenue?", model = "unpriced-model", trace = tr)
#> Warning: Model 'unpriced-model' has no price set, so the $5 spending limit
#> (max_cost_usd) does not cover its requests: they are sent, and the trace
#> records their cost as NA. Set its prices with hr_register_model(input_usd =,
#> output_usd =) or hr_load_models(). Token and call limits still apply.
#> hr_options(allow_unpriced = FALSE) refuses such requests instead. Shown once
#> per model per session.
res <- hr_call(backend, "What was revenue?", model = "unpriced-model", trace = tr)
hr_trace_cost(tr)[, c("model", "calls", "paid_in", "paid_out", "usd", "priced")]
#>            model calls paid_in paid_out usd priced
#> 1 unpriced-model     2      14       26  NA  FALSE

The two requests gave one warning. The trace counts their tokens and records their cost as NA. max_calls and max_tokens_total still hold such requests, and then max_tokens_total is the limit that bounds what a run spends.

allow_unpriced = FALSE refuses them instead. hr_call() then sends nothing and returns a failed result whose refusal is a condition of class hr_unpriced_model:

prev <- hr_options(allow_unpriced = FALSE)
res <- hr_call(backend, "What was revenue?", model = "unpriced-model",
               trace = hr_trace())
res$refused
#> [1] TRUE
class(res$refusal)
#> [1] "hr_unpriced_model" "hr_budget_refused" "condition"
hr_options(prev)

hr_governor(allow_unpriced = FALSE) does the same for one run. Under either, gr_read() stops before its first request, with an error of the same class. hr_mock_client() and replays are never refused or warned about for this, and neither is an embedding model with no price.

An hr_ellmer_client() is priced as the model its ellmer object was built with, whatever a recipe names, so set the price of that model. One built on a model with no price runs outside the spending limit. “Connecting to a model” in vignette("harnessr") registers a hosted model at its prices and a local one at zero.

When prices go stale

The prices you set go out of date too. A cost computed from prices older than price_max_age_days (120 days by default) warns with class hr_stale_price, once per model per session. The age counts from the first day of the as_of month. A file whose prices were checked in January 2025 shows it:

old_prices <- file.path(tempdir(), "models-guide-old.csv")
# Illustrative figures.
writeLines(c("id,input_usd,output_usd,as_of", "gpt-4.1,2,8,2025-01"), old_prices)
hr_load_models(old_prices)
hr_estimate_cost("gpt-4.1", 120000, 4000)
#> Warning: The prices of model 'gpt-4.1' are as of 2025-01, 695 days ago, more
#> than the 120 days of hr_options(price_max_age_days =). Check your provider's
#> current prices and set them with hr_register_model(input_usd =, output_usd =)
#> or hr_load_models(). Shown once per model per session.
#> [1] 0.272
hr_estimate_cost("gpt-4.1", 120000, 4000)
#> [1] 0.272

harnessr still returns the figure, and the second estimate does not warn again. To clear the warning, check your provider’s current prices and set every price the entry has again, cached_input_usd included when it has one: hr_register_model() then stamps the current month, and so does a row of hr_load_models() with a blank as_of. A change that leaves one of the entry’s prices out keeps the older month, and the warning stays, even when the row gives a newer as_of. A model with no price is never stale, and its as_of, the month its limits were checked, does not count.

Counting tokens

harnessr counts tokens in three places: to size a prompt before it is sent, to cut text to a number of tokens, and to fill in a usage figure the provider did not report. All three use hr_count_tokens():

txt <- c(prose = "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.",
         table = "| 2024 | 45.2 | 38.1 |",
         japanese = "東京は日本の首都です。",
         long_word = "pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis",
         blank = "")
hr_count_tokens(txt)
#> [1] 13 18 16 17  0

It returns one whole number per string, with blank and NA strings at 0.

How exact the default count is

hr_tokenizer() names the counter in use:

hr_tokenizer()
#> [1] "heuristic"

The default, "heuristic", needs nothing installed. It does not tokenize: it estimates, and it is built to come out high, because a count that comes out low lets a prompt past the window and the provider rejects the request after it has been paid for. It charges an ordinary English word at least one token, a dense string (an id, a number, code) one token per 1.3 characters, each character outside ASCII, such as Japanese or Cyrillic, 1.15 tokens, and an emoji 6.5. For tables, digit lists and short lines it also counts the pieces a byte-pair tokenizer splits text into first (digit groups, punctuation runs, line breaks) and keeps the larger figure, line by line. Each string that is not blank then gets 3 more tokens for the framing a chat message carries.

Measured against OpenAI’s cl100k_base and o200k_base encodings, it comes in at or above the real count on tables, digit lists, tab-separated text and short punctuated lines. Rare long words are where it can fall short: on a table of medical terms it came in about a tenth under. The safety_margin option, a tenth of the window by default, is the room hr_budget() leaves for that error.

The two other built-in counters are cruder. "words" counts words, and "chars" divides the characters by 4:

prev_tok <- hr_tokenizer()
counts <- sapply(c("heuristic", "words", "chars"), function(t) {
  hr_set_tokenizer(t)
  hr_count_tokens(txt[1:4])
})
rownames(counts) <- names(txt)[1:4]
counts
#>           heuristic words chars
#> prose            13     9    11
#> table            18     7     6
#> japanese         16     1     3
#> long_word        17     1    12
hr_set_tokenizer(prev_tok)

Both count below the heuristic on every row, and "chars" counts 11 Japanese characters as 3 tokens. A low count is the direction that overruns a window, so keep the heuristic unless you have a counter that matches your model.

Plugging in a real tokenizer

hr_set_tokenizer("tiktoken") switches to OpenAI’s tokenizer, through the reticulate package and Python’s tiktoken:

hr_set_tokenizer("tiktoken")
hr_count_tokens("The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.", model = "gpt-4o")

Given a model that tiktoken knows, it counts in that model’s encoding. Without one, which is how harnessr’s own budgets call it, it counts in both encodings current OpenAI models use (cl100k_base and o200k_base) and keeps the larger. For a model from another provider the count is an estimate with none of the heuristic’s padding. Without reticulate or tiktoken, hr_set_tokenizer("tiktoken") stops with an error and the tokenizer stays as it was: a silent fallback would change every budget without a word.

For any other model, register a counter of your own: a function that takes a character vector and returns one count per element. A provider’s tokenizer wrapped in R goes here. This one stands in for it with a rule of thumb of 3 characters per token:

hr_set_tokenizer("three_chars", function(x) ceiling(nchar(x) / 3))
hr_tokenizer()
#> [1] "three_chars"
hr_count_tokens(txt)
#> [1] 15  8  4 15  0

hr_set_tokenizer() registers the function under the name and makes it the active counter; from then on, hr_set_tokenizer("three_chars") switches back to it by name. The counter gets the text alone, not the model. harnessr sets a negative or NA count to 0, and stops if the function returns the wrong number of counts. A counter you register is copied to the workers of a parallel run, with the models you registered.

Switch back to the counter in use before, the default heuristic, for the rest of the guide:

hr_set_tokenizer(prev_tok)
hr_tokenizer()
#> [1] "heuristic"

Where a count shows up

A result’s usage says where its token counts came from. A backend that returns plain text reports none, so harnessr counted the prompt and the reply itself:

res <- hr_call(backend, "What was revenue?", model = "gpt-4o-mini")
str(res$usage)
#> List of 3
#>  $ input     : int 7
#>  $ output    : int 13
#>  $ provenance: chr "estimated"

provenance is "reported" when the provider gave the figures, "counted" when harnessr counted them with tiktoken, and "estimated" with any other counter, such as the heuristic that counted the prompt here as 7 tokens and the reply as 13. A count made with a crude counter can undercount a request’s cost, so an estimated usage is worth checking against the provider’s bill on a real run.

Choosing the settings

Four options decide how the registry and the counter behave. Each walkthrough says what the option controls, the signs that point to changing it, where its default came from, and how to test a change.

Unknown models: unknown_model_action

What it controls. What a lookup does when the registry does not hold the id: "warn" (the default) guesses from a family pattern or the default profile and warns with class gr_unknown_model; "error" stops with an error of that class, so no request goes out with guessed limits.

Signs it needs changing. A gr_unknown_model warning in a run you meant to send to a known model is a typo or a new model. On a scheduled or unattended run, set "error", since nobody reads the warning before the run spends.

Where the default came from. "warn" lets a first run with a new model work. gr_settings_table("options") declares no evidence for it.

How to test it. Look up every id a script uses under "error" before the run:

prev <- hr_options(unknown_model_action = "error")
ids <- c("gpt-4o", "chatgpt-4o-latest", "gpt-5.6-tera")
vapply(ids, function(id) {
  tryCatch(hr_model_info(id)$source, gr_unknown_model = function(e) "unknown")
}, "")
#>            gpt-4o chatgpt-4o-latest      gpt-5.6-tera 
#>      "registered"           "alias"         "unknown"
hr_options(prev)

Models with no price: allow_unpriced

What it controls. Whether a request to a chat model with no price is sent while max_cost_usd is set. TRUE, the default, sends it, records its cost as NA and warns once per model with class hr_unpriced_model. FALSE refuses it with a condition of that class.

Signs it needs changing. An hr_unpriced_model warning, or NA in the usd column of hr_trace_cost(), on a run whose cost has to stay under a limit. Set the model’s prices; set allow_unpriced = FALSE when a run must never spend outside the limit.

Where the default came from. harnessr ships no prices, so FALSE would refuse every request to a built-in model until you set its prices. gr_settings_table("options") lists it as untested.

How to test it. Check which models a run names have a price before you send anything:

run_models <- c("gpt-4o", "gpt-4o-mini", "unpriced-model")
do.call(rbind, lapply(run_models, hr_estimate_cost, input_tokens = 0, detail = TRUE))
#>            model usd priced   as_of certain
#> 1         gpt-4o   0   TRUE 2026-11    TRUE
#> 2    gpt-4o-mini   0   TRUE 2026-11    TRUE
#> 3 unpriced-model  NA  FALSE    <NA>    TRUE

How old a price may be: price_max_age_days

What it controls. The age in days, counted from the first day of a price’s as_of month, past which a cost computed from the price warns with class hr_stale_price. NULL turns the warning off. The warning changes no figure and stops nothing.

Signs it needs changing. A stale warning on prices you checked recently means the as_of in your file is behind; update it rather than the option. Raise the limit for a provider whose prices you know have not moved, such as a contract price.

Where the default came from. 120 days, about four months, so prices set once are checked again a few times a year. gr_settings_table("options") lists it as untested.

How to test it. hr_models() shows the month of every price, and the age in days follows from it:

m <- hr_models()
p <- m[!is.na(m$input_usd_per_1m), c("id", "as_of")]
p$age_days <- as.numeric(Sys.Date() - as.Date(paste0(p$as_of, "-01")))
p
#>               id   as_of age_days
#> 6        gpt-4.1 2025-01      695
#> 9         gpt-4o 2026-11       26
#> 10   gpt-4o-mini 2026-11       26
#> 19 gpt-5.6-terra 2026-11       26
#> 20   local-llama 2026-11       26
#> 21 partner-model 2026-10       57
#> 23 gateway-embed 2026-11       26

To see the option at work, load a price checked in January 2025 for a model no estimate has used yet, and estimate its cost under a higher limit and then under the default:

contract <- file.path(tempdir(), "models-guide-contract.csv")
# Illustrative figures.
writeLines(c("id,context_window,max_output,input_usd,output_usd,as_of",
             "contract-model,128000,4096,1,4,2025-01"), contract)
hr_load_models(contract)
prev_age <- hr_options(price_max_age_days = 3650)
hr_estimate_cost("contract-model", 100000, 2000)
#> [1] 0.108
hr_options(prev_age)
hr_estimate_cost("contract-model", 100000, 2000)
#> Warning: The prices of model 'contract-model' are as of 2025-01, 695 days ago,
#> more than the 120 days of hr_options(price_max_age_days =). Check your
#> provider's current prices and set them with hr_register_model(input_usd =,
#> output_usd =) or hr_load_models(). Shown once per model per session.
#> [1] 0.108

Under a limit of 3650 days the price is not stale and the first estimate gives no warning. Back at 120 days, the second warns. The figure is the same both times. hr_options(price_max_age_days = NULL) turns the check off.

The token counter: tokenizer

What it controls. Which counter hr_count_tokens() uses, and so every budget, every cut to a number of tokens and every usage figure the provider did not report. Set it with hr_set_tokenizer(), which checks the name and, for "tiktoken", that Python’s package is there.

Signs it needs changing. A provider error that a prompt was too long means the counter came in under. Usage marked "estimated" that differs much from the provider’s bill is the other sign. With OpenAI models and Python at hand, "tiktoken" gives exact counts.

Where the default came from. The heuristic needs nothing installed and is built to come out high; its calibration is described above. gr_settings_table("options") declares no evidence for it.

How to test it. Count a sample of your own text with each counter you consider, and compare the counts with the prompt tokens your provider reports for the same text:

sample_text <- c("Net revenue rose 12% to $45.2 million in fiscal 2024.",
                 "| segment | 2023 | 2024 |\n| retail | 38.1 | 45.2 |")
sapply(c("heuristic", "words", "chars"), function(t) {
  hr_set_tokenizer(t)
  hr_count_tokens(sample_text)
})
#>      heuristic words chars
#> [1,]        22    10    14
#> [2,]        27    14    13
hr_set_tokenizer(prev_tok)

The heuristic counts both texts highest, 22 and 27, since it is built to come out high; "words" and "chars" give 10 to 14. The counter whose figures sit closest above your provider’s reported prompt tokens is the one to keep.

Where the document layer builds on this

The segmenters size chunks with hr_count_tokens(), the readers fit each prompt to the model’s window from hr_model_info(), and every cost the document layer reports comes from these prices. vignette("runs") shows the costs a whole document run reports.
